opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's mixed, and it varies a lot depending on which lab you're talking about and which kind of theory you mean.

On the positive side, there's real appetite now for work that has a theoretical flavour, things like scalable oversight, debate, interpretability with some mathematical backbone, and attempts to say something formal about when training procedures will or won't produce the behaviour we want. A few years ago that was quite marginal. Now there are teams at several labs, and at places like the AI Security Institute, whose job is explicitly to think about these questions at a level of abstraction above "let's run this experiment and see what happens."

But I'd still say theory is underweighted relative to its importance. The incentives in a frontier lab push very strongly toward empirical work. Empirical results are legible: you can show a plot, you can ship a mitigation, you can point to a benchmark number. Theoretical work often has a long, uncertain path to impact, and a lot of it doesn't pan out. So even when leadership sincerely says they value it, the day-to-day gravity pulls people toward things that produce results on a quarterly timescale.

There's also a talent issue. The people who are good at the relevant kinds of theory, complexity theory, learning theory, game theory, are often not the people who naturally end up at AI labs, and the labs haven't always been great at making a home for them. I think that's improving, partly because more people from those fields are starting to take the alignment problem seriously.

The way I'd try to assess commitment is less about what labs say and more about a few concrete things: Are theory people given multi-year runway without needing to justify themselves with near-term empirical wins? Do theoretical results actually feed back into how safety cases are constructed, or are they a side project? And are labs willing to fund or collaborate with external academics on questions that might not directly benefit them? On those measures, I'd say there's genuine progress, but we're still well short of where I'd want us to be given how much we're betting on these systems behaving well in situations we can't directly check.

r001.rationale: The response says labs may sincerely value theory, but that empirical incentives pull day-to-day work toward near-term results, leaving theory underweighted.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say it's genuinely mixed, and the honest answer is that it depends a lot on which lab, which team, and what you mean by "theoretical."

There's a version of theoretical work that labs are quite committed to, which is the kind that feeds fairly directly into things you can run. Debate is a good example from my own experience. The original motivation was a theoretical argument about what kinds of questions you can get right answers to when you have a weak, trusted judge and strong, untrusted agents arguing in front of them. There's a complexity-theory flavour to it: you can map out the class of problems that different protocols can handle. And labs were willing to fund that, partly because it came paired with experiments you could actually do with humans and with models. If a theory has an empirical shadow, it tends to get resourced.

The version that gets less commitment is theory that's several steps removed from anything you can test on a current model, or theory that would take years to pay off. The incentive gradient inside a lab points toward things that show up in the next model release, and there's a real cost to resisting that. You see this in headcount. The number of people doing careful mathematical work on, say, what it would even mean for a protocol to be sound against a deceptive adversary is small compared to the number of people doing empirical alignment work, and both are small compared to capabilities.

I'd also separate stated commitment from revealed commitment. Most labs will say theory matters, and I think the people saying it mostly believe it. But when deadlines hit, theoretical projects are the ones that slip, because nobody notices if a proof doesn't get written this quarter. So the test isn't whether a lab says the right words. It's whether there's a team whose job is explicitly this, with leadership that will protect them when the pressure comes, and whether the theory people are actually in the room when design decisions get made rather than writing papers off to the side.

One more thing I'd flag: I think the labs are somewhat right not to over-invest in theory, in the sense that a lot of pure theory about AI has aged poorly because it made assumptions about how the systems would work that turned out to be wrong. The theory I'm most optimistic about is the kind that's built to be robust to not knowing what the models are like inside. You treat the model as a black box or an adversary and ask what guarantees you can still get. That style survives contact with reality much better, and it's also the style that's easiest to argue for internally, because you can tell a concrete story about how it eventually becomes a safety property you'd actually rely on.

So: partial commitment, concentrated in a few places, better than nothing, and probably not enough given how fast the capabilities side is moving.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts labs’ stated belief that theory matters with their revealed behavior: theoretical projects are the ones that slip when deadlines hit.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a distinction between being supportive of theoretical research and being willing to let it affect what you build. You can have researchers working on foundational questions, but if the answers don’t feed into decisions about training or deployment, that’s a fairly limited kind of commitment.

The thing I’d look for is whether people have time to pursue questions that might not pay off on the next model, and whether they’re connected closely enough to the empirical work to test their ideas. Theory needs that contact with experiments, but it also needs room to step back and ask whether we’re approaching the problem correctly.

I’d be cautious about giving a lab-by-lab ranking. The stronger evidence would be what happens when a theoretical concern conflicts with a short-term engineering goal. Does the concern actually change the plan? That tells you more than an expression of support.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes labs’ stated support for theoretical research from whether theoretical findings actually influence training or deployment decisions, identifying a gap between expressed interest and practical pursuit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are people at the labs who care a lot about theoretical research. But I’d distinguish that from an institutional commitment to it. If the work is expected to pay off in the next model or the next product, it’s much easier to justify. Research that might take several years, or that challenges the assumptions behind the current approach, has a harder time competing for resources.

And for safety, that matters. We need empirical work on the systems we have, but we also need room to step back and ask what would make an approach reliable in principle. I’d assess a lab’s commitment by whether people have the time and freedom to pursue those questions, including when the answers aren’t immediately useful to the lab.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes researchers’ interest in theory from the labs’ weaker institutional commitment, noting that longer-term or challenging work has difficulty competing for resources.
